image_description:
1. **Chart type**
- **Top:** Histogram of ring cost.
- **Bottom:** Horizontal bar chart showing share of income spent on an engagement ring by annual income group.

2. **Layout techniques**
- The visualization uses **two vertically stacked panels**.
- No faceting or small multiples are used.
- No stacking within bars; each panel is a single-series chart.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Ring cost | Quantitative | Position on x-axis (top histogram bins) |
| Number of people | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height in histogram |
| Annual income | Ordinal categorical | Position on y-axis (bottom horizontal bars), text labels |
| Share of income spent on an engagement ring | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis in bottom chart, text annotation |
| Time equivalent spent (e.g., weeks/months) | Quantitative | Text annotation at end of bars |
| Percentage in parentheses | Quantitative | Text annotation at end of bars |

comments.raw_comment:
Putting a Price on Love
It was interesting to take a look at how much people spend on engagement rings, and how much of their salary they're spending on an engagement ring. The thing I’ve always heard about pricing for rings is that you are supposed to spend 2 months of your salary on an engagement ring. The graph has a significant drop off after about $3,000 dollars. There are of course outliers for the incredibly wealthy, with a spike in the data at 15,000+. But what really interests me is that the second lower graph shows that the people spending two months salary on an engagement ring are those who make less than 23,000. While anyone making more only spends around 2 weeks salary.  I wonder if that puts more strain on a poorer couples relationship, or if it means more because of the effort put into having enough to buy an engagement ring?

I noticed that the information was different from logic's expectations. Usually, people with higher incomes would spend more on engagement rings since they have more money, while less well off consumers pay less. However, it was the complete opposite. Those with less than a $23,000 salary use 1/6 of their wages, while the highest income bracket of $90,000 spends 3.1%. I wonder if this is caused by hubris and humility. The latter might be arrogant and greedy, believing that they should keep most of their money and spend a little on a perceived small matter like engagement rings. On the other hand, those who can't live successful lives try to find other ways to live happily besides money, thus focusing on their partner. 

If I could create a catchy title for these two graphs, I would use "Engagement Rings Defy Logic!" This is due to the fact that while many believe it's important to have a significant other, the graph demonstrates that very little money is spent on it, and if a considerable amount is used, it is usually by people with low incomes.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  “Engagement Economy“ by Avery of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, North Carolina, “The Rings of Love Become the Rings of Pain" by Mohamed of Academy for Software Engineering, New York, “Engagement Rings, Hand Over 2 Weeks Salary” by Riley of Bush, and "The Price of a Promise" by Soren of Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, Feb. 13 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graphics, and a few Stat Nuggets.

The next graph will be released Friday, Feb. 21, with moderation on Wednesday, Feb. 26.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic --  contagious diseases.

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is married and does not have an engagement ring, and Jen Mueller of St. Louis, who is married with an engagement ring.

comments.raw_comment: The most noticeable aspect of this graph is that the majority of the sample set spend from $1K-$3K on rings, while few spend from $10K-$15K. Additionally, those who earn less than $23,000 annually will spend 16.7% of this income on a ring, which is 2.2 months worth of their earnings. Individuals who earn more than $90,000 only spend 3.1% of their income, meaning that only 1.6 weeks of their earnings go towards the engagement ring. By taking a step back from the graphical data, a class divide is emphasized largely through the part of the graph illustrating the percentage of their income that is spent on an engagement ring. Lower middle-class and lower-class people can be significantly harmed due to this institutionalized cultural value of purchasing an expensive physical manifestation of one’s love for their partner. This possible harm towards one’s financial well-being causes these rings’ importance to be questioned. If there was another socially acceptable way to propose to a loved one that did not cause one to spend 16.7% of their income, would there be a small percentage decrease in the class divide or low-income levels? This graph illustrates how much an adult will spend on an engagement ring. The majority of the population sampled spends between $1K-$3K on a ring. This trend could reflect on how many Americans can not afford to spend more than that range of money on a single physical object, while very few make enough annually to spend $10K or more on an engagement ring.

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the amount people spend on engagement rings, and the share of their income they spend on engagement rings based on their income.  Most people spend from 1 to 5 thousand dollars, with the most people spending less than 1 thousand. As the price goes up, the amount of people buying goes down. At first analysis of the provided graph from The New York Times, I noticed a graph that showed a decay or a depression. The graph compares the percentage of people from a study, and the amount the person spent on an engagement ring. The graph shows a prominent decay in the purchase of a ring as the price reaches an estimation of $2.5 thousand or $3 dollars. As the amount required to purchase the ring continues to increase the number of people willing to spend that amount decreases, which is until the final amount presented. At $15 thousand an increase of people that were able or even willing to purchase an engagement ring of that price.
	A more interesting aspect of the graph is the comparison of the annual income of an individual and the share of income spent on an engagement ring. The lower amount of income an individual made seemed to correlate how long they spent on either saving a ring or how long it would take to remake the amount they spend on a ring back. For example, an individual who made less than $23,000 a year would have to spend more than two months re-earning money back, whereas a person who made $23,000 to $40,000 would have to spend only two weeks.
	These graphs bring an interesting insight into the financial side of engagement rings and the financial impact they can have on an individual. While the meaning behind an engagement ring is typically more important than the financial worth, the impact of the cost is just as important as the meaning.

I noticed that most people spend a thousand dollars or less on engagement rings. I also noticed that the more expensive the engagement ring amounts to, the less likely people will buy it. People with a smaller income could likely be more inclined to make a more financial meager decision than the financial wealthy.

This means that if a person with  much larger income wants to buy an engagement ring, they will be more inclined to buy a more expensive ring because the cost of the ring would take up a smaller amount of the person's income.

In a post by New York Times, there is shown a graph visualizing the relation of the cost of engagement rings to how many people buy them. Something of immediate notice on this article as a whole is that the date shows that the data was posted on the 12th of February, 2020, a time which has not yet come to New York. The most notable part of the graph itself is that, as far as the data on the graph shows, people buy more cheaper rings rather than expensive ones. Which is understandable, rings are expensive in general. What is interesting in this data, however, is the fact that after a steady decline in purchases as prices rise, there is a spike in the amount of people buying rings for $15k+.
	A question as to what the reason is for this data comes to mind after seeing the anomalies in this graph. Because as expensive as engagement rings already are in general, it would make sense that people should not buy as many expensive rings as much as cheaper ones. Especially when considering that engagement rings are separate from wedding rings, some people may want to spend more on wedding rings because they may simply mean more to both the givers and receivers. Yet after a cost of 15 thousand dollars per ring, people start buying again.
